Die Yield, Three Resolutions

Predicting which dies survive the pre-test and then fail the post-test — and finding that the die measurements had nothing left to give, while the wafer they sit on had a great deal.

160 train, 40 held out. Each carries its own failure rate, drawn independently.

Result

Where the gain came from

Both models are scored by the same code, on the same wafer-grouped folds, against the same baseline that shipped with this repository. Model B improves average precision by 7.8% and fail-class F1 by 4.3%. Almost none of that comes from modelling the die measurements better, because there was nothing there to get.

Average precision on the minority class, five wafer-grouped folds repeated three times. The two additions are independent of each other and of the feature set.

Die resolution · what was already solved

The die measurements were finished before I started

The generator builds each of the 500 features by drawing from a normal distribution and adding a constant, fail_shift, to failing dies. That constant is a deterministic function of config.yaml, which means the exact likelihood-ratio direction can be written down rather than estimated — a genuine oracle, not a well-tuned model.

Scoring it gives AP 0.5271. The baseline's fitted Model A reaches 0.5137: 97% of the ceiling. Every remaining idea about the parametric block — better regularisation, interactions, a bigger model — was competing for the last 0.014, and a regularisation sweep across three orders of magnitude confirmed it, moving average precision by 0.002.

Measuring that first is what redirected the work. The reason so little is available is in the generator too: 65% of failures are marked marginal and receive only 5–25% of the shift, which puts them roughly one standard deviation from the passing population no matter how well they are modelled.

Die resolution · estimator, not features

500 independent measurements, 6,519 failures

Conditional on the label, each measurement is an independent draw. That makes the diagonal — naive-Bayes — discriminant the matched estimator: one mean difference per feature, rather than 500 coefficients fitted jointly against only 6,519 positive examples. Collapsing the parametric block to that single score and putting a small logistic head over it, alongside the spatial and block features, is the whole change.

It is worth +0.0131 AP on Model B and +0.0122 on Model A, and it fits about four times faster (47s against 184s) because there is no longer a 500-parameter joint optimisation in the loop. Gradient boosting on the identical inputs scores 0.5430 — below the flat logistic, at 31× the cost. When the true decision function is linear in standardised measurements, trees spend their capacity on noise.

Wafer resolution · the actual headroom

A rate you cannot predict, but can measure

generate_die_features draws wafer_base_rate from an exponential distribution and multiplies every die's hazard by it. It is independent of the wafer map, of the pre-test failures, of everything visible before the test — and it ranges from near zero to 25%. No feature predicts it, which is presumably why the baseline does not try.

But it does not need to be predicted. The scores on a single wafer are a two-component mixture — passing dies from one distribution, failing dies from another — and the mixing weight is that wafer's failure rate. It can be recovered by maximum likelihood from the wafer's own scores, using no labels at all, which means it is equally available on the unlabelled validation split. It then enters as a prior shift: 

logit_adjusted = logit + α × (logit(rate_wafer) − logit(rate_overall))

Reference densities are estimated leave-one-wafer-out, so a wafer's own labels never inform its own rate. On the held-out wafers the recovered rate tracks the real one at r = 0.895, and the step is worth +0.0346 AP — the largest single contribution here.

The shrinkage α matters more than it looks. At full strength the correction assumes the recovered rate is exact. It is not: a wafer of ~950 dies at a 2% rate carries about 19 failures, and in log-odds a factor-of-two error there is a shift of 0.7 — comparable to the entire spread of the die-level score. Unshrunk, it lifted AP but cost F1 outright (0.5258 → 0.5091). At α = 0.5, chosen on training out-of-fold scores, both improve.

Rejected

Two ideas that did not survive contact

Both are kept in the repository with the evidence, because on a problem this close to its ceiling, knowing which plausible ideas are dead is most of the result.

Rejected · costs 0.021 AP

Removing the per-wafer process gradient

Every feature carries a radial and a linear gradient whose coefficients are redrawn for each wafer, and those gradients lie exactly in the span of [1, x, y, radius]. Regressing them out within each wafer looks unambiguously correct, and on synthetic wafers with uniformly scattered defects it is.

On real WM-811K maps it is not. The new failures are themselves clustered against radius and against pre-test defect neighbourhoods, so the regression absorbs signal along with the nuisance. Scored with the generator's own coefficients, average precision falls from 0.5271 raw to 0.5065 detrended — and the wafer-rate recovery degrades badly too (r 0.888 → 0.500), because removing the per-wafer intercept removes the very offset the mixture reads.

Rejected as a gain · kept for interpretability

Matched-filter block scans

The block anomalies are roughly 100 positive spikes clustered around one seed with a spread of 0.05 × k, which makes a circular Gaussian scan the matched detector and the baseline's boxcar sums an approximation to it. Head-to-head on identical rows, folds and classifier: AP 0.1321 against 0.1296, using 27 columns instead of 53.

That is a tie. An earlier read of mine claimed a real gain here; it was comparing my linear model against the baseline's boosted one, so the gap was the classifier, not the features. The scan is kept because its peak names which block region is anomalous, which the interpretability output needs — not because it predicts better.

Block resolution · Model A → Model B

What the sub-die data actually adds

Block readings alone reach AP 0.1372 against a 4.23% base rate — weak, but far from nothing. Their value is that they are informative about exactly the dies the parametric features cannot see. The generator injects the block signature into every failing die, marginal or not, while the parametric shift for a marginal failure is scaled down to 5–25%. So the block channel is the only die-level evidence for the majority of failures.

That shows up in the delta: adding block data moves Model A from 0.5524 to 0.6209, +0.0685 AP, a wider gap than the baseline's +0.0621. The right panel below is the direct test — among true failures ranked poorly by Model A, how many does Model B pull into the top 5%.

Interpretability

The attribution is the model, not a summary of it

Both models are linear in standardised inputs, and the stacked model is a linear head over a linear score, so the composition stays exactly additive. For any die the log-odds decompose with no sampling, no surrogate model and no approximation error: 

logit(p) = intercept + parametric terms + spatial terms + block terms

The test suite asserts that decomposition sums back to predict_proba to within 1e-6 for both model forms, so the claim is checked rather than asserted. Per predicted failure that yields the measurements that drove it and by how much, the neighbourhood contribution, and the block-scan peak with its block range.

Laid back onto the wafer grid, the same decomposition gives one heatmap per resolution — so a cluster driven by neighbourhood effects looks visibly different from one driven by a die's own parameters, which is the distinction an engineer chasing root cause actually needs.

Class imbalance

4.23% positives, and no free lunch from accuracy

Predicting "all pass" scores 95.8% accuracy and zero recall, so accuracy is reported only for completeness. The pipeline handles the imbalance in four specific places:

  • folds are grouped by wafer_id and stratified, so no wafer is split across training and validation and every reported rate is a real held-out one;
  • the minority class is weighted by sqrt(negatives/positives) — full balanced weighting pushes the boundary well past the F1 optimum;
  • the decision threshold is chosen on out-of-fold predictions only, never on the data it is then scored against;
  • dies that already failed the pre-test are excluded from fitting and scoring entirely, and only re-attached as certain failures when the submission is assembled.

The operationally honest view is the second panel: with a fixed inspection budget, what share of true failures does a fab actually catch.
